🇷🇺🇮🇳⚡ According to reports, Russia has offered India its most advanced air and missile defense system, the S-500, but with additional conditions attached to the proposed purchase agreement, which could complicate India’s already ambitious plans to modernize its armed forces. Russia wants a minimum order of five S-500 regiments.
India, which is seeking to eliminate critical gaps in its air defense system, is considering acquiring five more S-400 systems, almost a decade after signing the initial agreement with Moscow. Despite the long wait, Russia has still not completed deliveries under the original contract, and the fifth S-400 system remains undelivered.
Meanwhile, India’s Ministry of Defence is also considering the acquisition of one or two S-500 systems to strengthen its strategic defenses, in particular through advanced missile defense and anti-satellite weapons.
However, the new conditions put forward by the Kremlin threaten to increase pressure on India’s already overstretched defense budget.
At the same time, New Delhi is pursuing several major procurement programs, including:
⬛ 114 Rafale fighter jets, as well as Rafale-M aircraft for Indian Navy aircraft carriers.
⬛ Submarines with air‑independent propulsion (AIP) to strengthen its undersea warfare capabilities.
⬛ Large-scale replenishment of missile and ammunition stocks, after significant losses in the May conflict with Pakistan, when Pakistani strikes destroyed substantial amounts of military supplies at Indian ammunition depots, including the depot in Beas.
With several costly defense procurements competing for limited financial resources, the conditions set by Moscow for the S-500 deal may force New Delhi to make difficult procurement decisions, potentially delaying plans to build a more comprehensive, multilayered air and missile defense system.
This situation also underscores India’s continued dependence on Russian defense technologies, despite delivery delays, rising procurement costs, and competing military priorities that complicate its long-term modernization ambitions.

👁 Pentagon builds secret tech agency to hack, deceive and sabotage foreign rivals - report
The Technology Support Office (TSO) is an elite tech agency geared to expanding covert efforts that targets foreign military technology programs seen as threatening US military dominance, Politico reports. 
Established in April, it has not been publicly acknowledged by War Secretary Pete Hegseth or other senior Pentagon officials.
Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, a private-equity billionaire and former Trump-era intelligence adviser, is said to have driven its formation with help from Tom Rakusan, a longtime CIA clandestine veteran.
TSO reportedly expands two smaller classified Pentagon programs that have conducted similar tech-sabotage work since 2023. 
Key features and aims:
➡️ close collaboration with military and intelligence officers to design tools that disrupt or subvert foreign defense technologies, particularly AI-powered systems and drones
➡️ workforce of engineers, special operators and intelligence officers building custom hacking tools and deception schemes, such as tricking adversaries into installing flawed components in weapons systems
➡️ efforts to streamline technology adoption across fragmented Pentagon intelligence programs, including a planned central catalog of approved commercial AI and tech tools for classified work

🇮🇱 Israel squeezes Gaza and the West Bank as elections loom
Palestinians in Gaza see their suffering reduced to campaign material ahead of Israel's October 27 election, with little expectation that the vote will change their reality, The Guardian reports.
Both Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition and his main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party, have centered their campaigns on destroying Hamas and responding to the trauma of October 7. Meanwhile, the devastation of Gaza — home to nearly a million displaced people facing dire sanitation, water shortages, and constant strikes — has gone almost unmentioned by either camp, and neither has outlined a clear plan for the territory's future.
The current government is not waiting for the vote to reshape the West Bank. After a shooting near Hebron killed two Israeli soldiers, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz announced plans to forcibly displace Palestinian residents and carry out extensive destruction, invoking the "offensive model" used in northern West Bank refugee camps that already displaced more than 33,000 people.
Arab-led parties are the sole political force addressing Palestinian suffering in their campaigns, but they are expected to play a marginal role in the next government, aligning with different camps rather than shaping policy.
Meanwhile, Gazans are now desperately short of basic necessities.
♦️ Warehouses across the Strip have completely run out of flour, and the seven remaining operational bakeries warned they could shut within 48 hours without new supplies
♦️ The World Food Programme has cut assistance to more than half a million people due to funding shortages, while crossings have been closed at various points during October, worsening restrictions on food, fuel, and aid
♦️ Families now face long queues for bread, with many returning home empty-handed, as warnings mount over the risk of famine returning to the besieged territory

events.text:
🇨🇳 China puts radar arrays in the wings inside aircraft to build a drone early-warning network
Chinese engineers from Chengdu Aircraft Design and Research Institute have put forward a concept that would place large antenna arrays directly into aircraft wings.
Fighter jets usually carry their main radar behind a nose cone, while traditional airborne early-warning aircraft mount large radar arrays in prominent structures above the fuselage. Wings offer a large surface area but are relatively thin, leaving little internal room for radar equipment.
The researchers argue that the future of distributed air combat will require many smaller, cheaper unmanned aircraft working together rather than a single large platform. That creates a technical challenge: achieving large-scale detection with relatively small individual platforms.
How the wing-mounted radar would work
🔶 The radar antenna is built directly into the wing itself, facing downward, with a cover that follows the wing's shape — this gives the radar a much larger surface to work with than a nose-mounted system, without needing a big external dome
🔶 To point the radar in a different direction, the aircraft simply changes its flight attitude, which tilts the wing-mounted antenna to a different position
🔶 The study outlines the system could operate in different ways, including scanning in all directions, scanning in several directions at once, and several aircraft working together — either spreading out to cover a wide area, focusing on a specific target, or joining forces to resist enemy jamming
🔶 Having multiple aircraft detect targets together is described as the key to the whole "small platforms, big capabilities" idea
 
A distributed network of wing-mounted radars on cheaper unmanned platforms would be harder to disable with a single strike and could extend coverage across the vast distances of the Indo-Pacific without relying on a handful of high-value targets.

🇪🇺 Europe’s cost-of-living anger spills into streets as protests turn violent across several countries
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied across France for a second straight weekend amid anger over living costs and deteriorating public services. Similar grievances also fueled protests that swept Italy, Portugal and Albania.
Despite curfews and restrictions imposed in more than 100 French cities, clashes erupted, though the destruction was less extensive than last weekend.
🔴 authorities deployed 70,000 police backed by armored vehicles, water cannons and drones
🔴 government counted 410,000 demonstrators, compared with 800,000 estimated by the CGT union
🔴 around 1,000 people detained nationwide by Saturday evening, two were seriously injured
🔴 police deployed water cannon in Paris 
🔴 clashes broke out in Lyon, Lille, Nice, Rennes and Dijon, with police deploying tear gas; some stores were damaged or looted
In Italy, demonstrations turned violent in Turin, Rome and Bologna, while protests in Milan remained largely peaceful. 
In Portugal, police dismantled a protest camp in Lisbon after thousands marched over soaring rents, housing unaffordability, and proposed changes that would ease evictions and lift rent caps on new leases. 
[Albania’s student-led protests ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76384)over government corruption, unemployment and poor education standards escalated in Tirana. 
Police used tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets as demonstrators hurled rocks and set fire to the agriculture ministry entrance, demanding PM Edi Rama’s resignation.
